articles.title: Tension and clashes as hundreds of thousands protest again in France
articles.text:
Tension and clashes as hundreds of thousands protest again in France | Protests News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Protesters use makeshift shields during a demonstration in Paris, France, on Saturday [Pedro Nunes/Reuters]
By Al Jazeera Staff and AFP
Published On 31 Oct 202631 Oct 2026
Police have fired tear gas at protesters in Paris and Lyon as hundreds of thousands of mostly young people marched across France over the cost of living and the state of the country’s schools.
Saturday’s rallies were the third consecutive weekend of demonstrations in France.
Recommended Stories list of 4 items
list 1 of 4 UN experts sound alarm at excessive use of force in French student protests
list 2 of 4 France braces for ‘very high risk’ of disorder at Halloween protests
list 3 of 4 Italy tightens security as students, unions launch nationwide protests
list 4 of 4 Polish police deployed to top court after head judge suspendedend of list
A coalition of youth organisations and unions representing high school and university students said nearly half a million people took part, including 200,000 in Paris. The authorities put the nationwide turnout at 320,000, including 70,000 in the capital.
Marches in the capital began peacefully, but turned violent as protesters gathered near the point where the main march was due to end on Saturday. Bins and street furniture were set alight, and plumes of smoke could be seen rising over the city.
“What we’ve been seeing … is the police firing a lot of tear gas into this crowd,” said Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler, reporting from Paris, adding that her team “had to move out of the way because it was simply too much for us to breathe”.
Riot police warned over loudspeakers that they would fire more tear gas if protesters did not clear the street. Medics carried away people who had been injured, while some protesters raised their hands to show police they meant no harm.
Dozens of masked people dressed in black also used hammers to pry up paving stones and hurl them at police on the outskirts of Paris, the AFP news agency reported. At least one incendiary device was also thrown at security forces, who responded with tear gas and baton charges.
Advertisement
France’s Ministry of Interior said at least 290 people nationwide had so far been arrested.
A police officer holds a Cougar grenade launcher in Toulouse, southwestern France [AFP]
Protesters say ‘trust has gone’
Butler said most protesters condemned the violence, but many blamed the government for failing to listen to them.
“You really get a sense with people who have come into the street again and again over the past few weeks that they simply don’t believe the government any more. That trust has gone,” she said.
The government says it has heard the protesters. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has held several meetings with student unions this week and is looking at measures to ease the cost of living.
About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country, and Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned of a “very high risk” of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween.
The main Paris march was moved to the city’s eastern edge after a last-minute court battle, and unaccompanied minors faced a 9pm (20:00 GMT) curfew around the Champs-Elysees.
The movement began last month with high school students protesting against neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labour unions have since joined.
Rallies spread across Europe
On October 17, protests drew more than 500,000 people and turned into some of France’s worst rioting in years, according to government estimates, with shops in Paris looted.
Meanwhile, protests have taken place in other cities across Europe.
On Saturday, young people in Germany were the latest to join the fray.
Thousands rallied while police in Cologne used water cannon to break up large crowds protesting against rising costs, education cuts and plans for military conscription. Organisers said 170,000 people had registered for demonstrations in more than 30 cities.
In Barcelona, Spain, regional police prepared their highest alert level after rioting on October 24 led to about 130 arrests, mostly of minors.
Italian police were also on alert after clashes in Milan, Turin and Bologna.
A protester holds a firework during a demonstration in Paris, France [Pedro Nunes/Reuters]

articles.title: London police arrest 48 as hundreds protest Palestine Action ban
articles.text:
London police arrest 48 as hundreds protest Palestine Action ban | Israel-Palestine conflict News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
A pro-Palestinian activist is carried away by police officers after being arrested during a protest outside the US embassy in London on Saturday [AFP]
By Al Jazeera Staff
Published On 31 Oct 202631 Oct 2026
Police have arrested at least 48 people after protesters defied a warning not to attend a rally in London against the proscription of Palestine Action, which is classified as a “terrorist” organisation under United Kingdom law.
Hundreds of people gathered outside the United States embassy on Saturday to oppose the ban, which came into effect in July last year under the government of then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 Ethnic cleansing fears rise as Israel squeezes space in Gaza: UN
list 2 of 3 Fans voice support on final night of Macklemore’s ‘Free Palestine’ tour
list 3 of 3 A UN protection force must be urgently deployed to Palestineend of list
The demonstration comes ahead of a Supreme Court appeal on Wednesday challenging the campaign group’s proscription.
“So far this afternoon, officers have arrested 48 people,” London’s Metropolitan Police said in a statement posted on X. “The majority of arrests have been for expressing support for a proscribed organisation. Officers remain at the scene and are continuing to make arrests.”
Responding to the police statement, Labour Party MP John McDonnell posted on X, saying someone protesting against the government’s decision to proscribe an organisation cannot be “automatically interpreted” as them supporting that organisation and “therefore committing an arrestable offence”.
He added that he believes the government “made the wrong decision in proscribing Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation”.
Saturday’s rally is the first mass protest against the proscription since Prime Minister Andy Burnham assumed office in July.
The decision to designate the group a “terrorist” organisation has triggered uproar among sections of British society, with critics arguing that it is part of a wider crackdown aimed at silencing pro-Palestine voices. The proscription means Palestine Action has been added to a list of banned organisations that also includes al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS).
UK ‘appeasing Trump and Israeli weapons companies’
Protesters also gathered outside the US consulate in Edinburgh, the Scottish capital. There have been no reports of arrests there.
Advertisement
Demonstrators in both London and Edinburgh could be seen holding placards reading “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action”.
Defend Our Juries, which organised the protests, said Saturday’s arrests took the total number of people detained for defying the Palestine Action ban to more than 4,000 since July 2025.
“It is truly dystopian that there have now been over 4,000 arrests under terror laws for peaceful vigils silently expressing opposition to genocide and support for the protest group Palestine Action,” a spokesperson for the group said, as reported by UK news agency Press Association.
“The ban on Palestine Action was straight out of [US President Donald] Trump’s playbook, so it’s fitting that this significant milestone has been reached on Halloween and outside the US embassy,” the spokesperson added, saying the proscription was about the UK government “appeasing Trump and the Israeli weapons companies that Palestine Action disrupted, not about any kind of terrorist threat”.
Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK’s head of communications and campaigns, also called on the government to reverse Palestine Action’s proscription.
“The sight yet again of grandparents, teenagers and everyone in between being hauled into police vans for peacefully holding placards is a disgraceful attack on freedom of speech,” Jakens said in response to the arrests on Saturday.
“It’s past time for the government to drop the proscription of Palestine Action and reform our laws so that communities have more power to demonstrate on the issues they care about, not less.”

articles.title: Thousands rally in Berlin as Gen Z plans protests in 30 German cities
articles.text:
Thousands rally in Berlin as Gen Z plans protests in 30 German cities | Protests News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Phil Tziartzianis travelled 8 hours to join his friend Jan Chrominski and other protesters in Berlin on Saturday [Giulio Ferracuti/Al Jazeera]
By Gouri Sharma
Published On 31 Oct 202631 Oct 2026
Berlin, Germany – Thousands of people are gathering in Berlin and more than 30 other German cities as the nation becomes the latest European country to be hit by a wave of student protests sweeping the continent.
Gathering at the Platz des 18 Maerz, on the west side of the capital’s iconic Brandenburg Gate on a sunny but chilly Saturday afternoon, there was support for the young people within a mixed demographic crowd.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 France braces for ‘very high risk’ of disorder at Halloween protests
list 2 of 3 Thousands protest across Italy over living costs and military spending
list 3 of 3 Protest at India university where no students’ union vote held for 20 yearsend of list
Anti-fascist activists smoking hand-rolled cigarettes and wearing keffiyehs waited patiently alongside students dressed in Halloween outfits, smartly dressed grandmothers donning “omas gegen rechts” (grandmothers against the right) badges, and camera crews, ahead of the 2pm (13:00 GMT) rally start.
The protests were organised by a loose alliance called Gen Z Regelt (Gen Z sorts it), and by Saturday morning, nearly 180,000 people across 34 cities had signed up to participate – with the main host cities including Frankfurt, Cologne, Munich and the capital Berlin.
Nearly 12,000 people had signed up to join in the German capital, and people were continuing to stream into the square well into the demonstration to listen to speakers in what was so far a calm afternoon in the capital.
However, at a rally in the western city of Cologne, scuffles broke out between protesters and police, who moved in to contain a march there.
The protest organisers had outlined six key issues that took them to the streets on Saturday, including the rising cost of living, education cuts and military conscription.
Student Veronika Dinter says she is angry that the government is increasing military spending even as it makes cuts to other areas like education [Giulio Ferracuti/Al Jazeera]
‘Political failure’ of government
Students told Al Jazeera that they are both angry and frustrated by ongoing funding cuts, even as the government invests heavily in the military.
Advertisement
Yet they also said they feel a sense of hope after seeing student protests in different parts of Europe in recent weeks.
Veronika Dinter travelled to Berlin on Friday night from Hannover to participate in the protest.
The 23-year-old political science student said that due to high living costs, she had to take on a part-time job to fund her studies.
“I wanted to start studying to develop critical thinking and learn something new, but I didn’t realise how much it would cost to do so. I think this is something a lot of people in my generation are experiencing right now,” she said.
“Funding for education and social services are being cut, while the cost of living keeps rising. Universities are struggling, institutes are closing, teachers are losing their jobs and education facilities are literally falling apart.
“This crisis is the political failure of our government. And instead of solving it, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his rich friends are funding the military with billions of euros.”
This is a sentiment that Emma Heymann, a 24-year-old student living in Berlin, resonated with.
“Our generation feels very angry at the government because they are making these huge cuts that are affecting our quality of life here. And at the same time, they are spending billions on the military and spending money to fund the genocide in Gaza,” she said.
Emma Heymann says her generation feels very angry about the way the government is impacting their quality of life [Giulio Ferracuti/Al Jazeera]
Protesters should be ‘listened to’
Phil Tziartzianis travelled eight hours from his hometown of Kassel to join his friend Jan Chrominski and other young people at the demonstration.
“It feels important for me to be here among other young people who feel the same way,” he said.
The protesters join a wave of demonstrations that have swept across Europe in recent weeks, including in France, Belgium, Italy, Spain and Serbia.
Kilian Hampel is a senior research fellow at the Future of Work Lab at the University of Konstanz. He says other demonstrations are having an impact on young Germans.
“The frustration itself has been building for years, but this is definitely part of a wave we are seeing across Europe, and young people here are feeling that they can actually take their worries and problems to the streets,” he said. “Many of their concerns, in particular around poor educational infrastructure, are legitimate, and it’s important that they are listened to.”
The Berlin demonstration is expected to last two hours, with another one organised by a different alliance, planned at 5:30pm (16:30 GMT) in a different part of the German capital.
Advertisement
In the past week, political figures have raised concerns about the protests turning violent.
Yet demonstrators say they see the narrative of violence distracting from the issues they want to raise.
“We urge the police to not confront our demonstrations with any kind of violence,” Dinter, the student from Hannover, said.
“We stand in solidarity with all the people around the world who are fighting for an affordable life, for more investment in the education system, and against wars and military buildup.”
Advertisement

articles.title: At least four Palestinians killed in Gaza as Israeli attacks continue
articles.text:
At least four Palestinians killed in Gaza as Israeli attacks continue | Israel-Palestine conflict News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Residents search the rubble for belongings following an Israeli strike in the Bureij refugee camp, in the central Gaza Strip, on October 30, 2026 [AFP]
By Anadolu
Published On 31 Oct 202631 Oct 2026
At least four Palestinians in Gaza have been killed as Israel continues to attack the enclave, despite a so-called “ceasefire” that has been in place for over a year.
Israel carried out several attacks in Gaza on Saturday, including shelling the Nuseirat refugee camp, in which Palestinian teacher Diaa Abu al-Rous was killed, al-Awda Hospital confirmed.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 Israel demolishes homes of Palestinians blamed for attack on soldiers
list 2 of 3 Education under fire: Gaza’s children face death on their way to school
list 3 of 3 Israel voted for Israel: Why Gaza wasn’t on the ballotend of list
Separately, another man, Arafat al-Arair, died after sustaining serious injuries days earlier when Israel struck a vehicle in the Tel al-Hawa neighbourhood, southwest of Gaza City. A medical source at al-Shifa Hospital confirmed his death.
Meanwhile, two girls also died on Saturday from injuries sustained the previous evening when their tent caught fire at a camp for displaced people in al-Mawasi, in Khan Younis. Nasser Medical Complex confirmed their deaths. It is not clear what caused the fire.
At least six Palestinians were killed in Gaza over the past 48 hours, according to the enclave’s Ministry of Health, bringing the number of people killed since the October 2025 ceasefire to 1,580.
In its daily statistical report on Saturday, the ministry said another 26 people were injured over the same period.
The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) warned on Friday that Israeli forces in Gaza were continuing to displace Palestinians and that their actions continued to raise concerns of ethnic cleansing.
The OHCHR said in a statement that Palestinians were increasingly being forced into a shrinking area of the territory, which has been decimated following three years of Israeli siege.
Advertisement
The office said Israeli forces were destroying what remained of Gaza’s civilian infrastructure. The Israeli military is working to expand its control over Gaza’s territory to 70 percent, following an order from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in May.
Reporting from Deir el-Balah, Al Jazeera’s Tareq Abu Azzoum said Israel was targeting civilians as it sought to displace Palestinians from the city.
“We have testimonies from people who have evacuated their homes in the eastern part of Deir el-Balah city, confirming that the Israeli military has adjusted the yellow demarcation line by opening fire on civilians to push them from these areas,” Abu Azzoum said.
Since a nominal “ceasefire” came into effect a year ago, Israeli attacks have killed at least 1,580 Palestinians and injured 5,711 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Talks aimed at permanently ending Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza under United States President Donald Trump’s peace plan have stalled. Reconstruction efforts have yet to begin amid disputes between Hamas and Israel over the implementation of Trump’s plan.
Hamas says it will not fully disarm until Israel withdraws entirely from Gaza. However, Israel maintains it will not leave the territory until Hamas forfeits its weapons.

articles.title: Dakar Youth Olympics: Who gets to hold the flame?
articles.text:
Dakar Youth Olympics: Who gets to hold the flame? | Olympics News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
A man runs past a mural of Dakar 2026 as Senegal prepares to host the Youth Olympic Games, the first Olympic event to be held in Africa, in Dakar [Misper Apawu/Reuters]
By Nicolas Haque
Published On 31 Oct 202631 Oct 2026
Dakar, Senegal – Senegal’s teenage volleyball players were training, giving everything they had. And I could see it in their eyes: the flame, that desire to win.
I was with my daughter and could see the effect it had on her: watching another girl her age play for a team, for a chance at gold, for something bigger than herself.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 Olympic flame arrives in Senegal for first ever Olympic event in Africa
list 2 of 3 The return of Palestinian football: ‘We are a people who must live’
list 3 of 3 South Africa centre bid in Durban for first Olympic Games on the continentend of list
I saw it again when my daughter helped a young boxer wrap her hands, before the fighter slipped on her gloves and threw a punch few adults could withstand, and when she helped a rowing captain into the water.
There is an ease with which teenagers find one another, a friendliness adults seem to have forgotten.
And so the 2026 Youth Olympic Games opening on the world’s youngest continent on Saturday feels fitting, particularly in this sports-crazy city I call home.
Looking around Dakar, almost everyone looks like an athlete.
Surfers paddle out at dawn. Children play basketball and football in the streets. Teenagers wrestle on beaches; others swim towards Ngor Island at breakneck speed. Construction workers, after a day’s labour, gather not in pubs or bars, but on the beach – to train, laugh and listen to music.
Sport is a way of life, but also a reason to be together.
For many in Dakar, visas and money make travel beyond their borders difficult. This time the world has come to them.
The Games were supposed to take place in 2022. Then came COVID-19, and Senegal’s then-president, Macky Sall, asked for more time to prepare. The Olympics would have to wait four years.
Advertisement
In an interview with Al Jazeera, Kirsty Coventry, the Zimbabwean former swimmer and Olympic gold medallist who now leads the International Olympic Committee, described it as a chance for Dakar, Senegal and Africa “to actually show what we’re capable of” – not merely tell the world.
Defying the odds
Senegal, meanwhile, is facing political and financial turmoil.
Billions of dollars of previously undisclosed debt have brought repeated credit downgrades, and the government is negotiating with creditors and the International Monetary Fund.
In a country where money is scarce, the question of what it costs to welcome the world cannot be separated from what the Games will leave behind.
Dakar can feel half built, its concrete exposed, its roads unfinished. Yet the city has done what it can with what it has. Christmas lights have become Olympic rings; and empty water bottles painted in the colours of visiting nations line roads leading towards refurbished venues.
I asked Coventry whether a country had to be wealthy to host an Olympic event.
“No,” she replied. The movement, she explained, needed to make the Games less complex and more affordable, using existing venues rather than demanding new ones.
Senegal’s influencer and TikToker Khaby Lame carries the Youth Olympic Flame on the eve of the opening ceremony of the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar on October 30, 2026 [AFP]
Despite Senegal’s debt and political turmoil, the land of teranga, of hospitality, is ready to welcome some 2,700 athletes and their parents, coaches and supporters. Some have never been to Africa. Expectations are being tested, sometimes quietly, in encounters no opening ceremony could arrange.
The Olympic flame, meanwhile, has passed from hand to hand. Khaby Lame, the TikTok star known for making millions laugh without speaking, carried it through Dakar. Then came Omar Sy, the actor who plays a thief in Lupin, running through his Senegalese father’s homeland, not like a thief but like a man who belonged, carrying something he was meant to give away.
Online, the jokes from locals came quickly: Would the electricity company embarrass Senegal with a power cut? Why are some business leaders so eager to hold the flame at Games meant for teenagers? Why do adults always want to hog the limelight…?
And increasingly, the Games are unfolding on mobile phones. Athletes film themselves opening their kit, boarding planes, arriving in Dakar, sharing what they find.
Australia has sent 41 teenagers on a journey of more than 24 hours. Britain’s young coastal rowers are preparing to race. Six refugee athletes, based in Africa, are competing under a flag of their own. These teenagers are their own broadcasters, their own brands.
Advertisement
Already, politics has slipped into the Games. Ukraine’s public broadcaster has refused to show the ceremonies because Russian and Belarusian teenagers will compete under their national flags.
The values Coventry spoke of – friendship, excellence, respect and the ideal of neutrality – are harder for adults to practise than to pronounce.
But politics has long accompanied the Games.
Jesse Owens won four gold medals in Hitler’s Berlin in 1936, the year the modern torch relay began. In 1968, Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised black-gloved fists on the podium in Mexico City, protesting racial injustice and poverty.
Pierre de Coubertin, the French founder of the modern Olympic movement, once spoke of sport’s “conquest” of Africa. In Paris in 1900, Haitian-born rugby player Constantin Henriquez became the first known Black Olympic gold medallist.
Extending gloved hands skyward in racial protest, US athletes Tommie Smith, centre, and John Carlos stare downward after Smith received the gold and Carlos the bronze in Mexico City in 1968 [File: AP]
Bigger than sport
It took more than a hundred years for the flame to come to Africa

articles.title: Iran FM says US outreach a ‘positive step’ as delegation in Qatar for talks
articles.text:
Iran FM says US outreach a ‘positive step’ as delegation in Qatar for talks | US-Israel war on Iran News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi [File: Elke Scholiers/Getty]
By Al Jazeera Staff
Published On 31 Oct 202631 Oct 2026
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says a United States effort to open dialogue with Tehran is “a positive step”, but that there are currently no plans for meetings with US officials regarding the eight-month-old war.
Speaking to Al Jazeera on Saturday, Araghchi said Iran had studied a letter sent by US Vice President JD Vance in high-level meetings, and set out Tehran’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which he said would pave the way for renewed negotiations with Washington.
Recommended Stories list of 4 items
list 1 of 4 Oman rescues 25 from burning oil tanker in Strait of Hormuz
list 2 of 4 Iran says four tankers on fire after striking mines in Hormuz
list 3 of 4 US greenlights $2.1bn Patriot missile sale to Ukraine
list 4 of 4 After the ‘martyr’s’ funeral: The families left behind by Yemen’s warend of list
He added that an Iranian delegation has travelled to Doha, a day after Qatari mediators were in Tehran in an apparent bid to negotiate a revival of the US-Iran ceasefire. Araghchi said one of his aides is in Qatar to continue consultations.
“The American side’s attempt to open the door to dialogue and understanding more broadly is a positive step,” the foreign minister told Al Jazeera.
However, he warned: “If Washington’s goal in sending this letter is to stir up discord, it would be yet another mistake to add to its previous ones.”
‘No need to meet with the Americans’
Araghchi played down talk of upcoming meetings between the two sides.
“What is being circulated in this regard is merely media speculation,” he said.
“We see no need to meet with the Americans at this stage. Our conditions are clear, and mediators are continuing their consultations regarding them,” he added.
Araghchi said whether Iran would hold direct or indirect talks with the US depended on Tehran’s conditions being met.
Advertisement
“Mediators have presented proposals concerning the nuclear dossier, which we are currently reviewing as part of the second phase,” he said.
“Qatari and Pakistani mediators are continuing consultations regarding our conditions,” he said.
Rouzbeh Parsi, an Iran analyst and affiliated researcher at Lund University’s Department of History and Human Rights Studies, told Al Jazeera that any progress in Friday’s talks in Tehran was most likely on “the sequencing of the first steps needed to establish the barest of trust – without which further bolder steps are not possible”.
Conditions for Hormuz
Araghchi said talks with Qatari mediators had shortened the time needed to implement Iran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
“The Qatari side proposed shortening the implementation period of the Iranian proposal to five days. We have reached a proposal at this stage that reduces the implementation period to two days,” he said.
“Our conditions include lifting the sanctions imposed following the Islamabad memorandum and reducing US forces in the region,” he said, adding, “We demand the restoration of oil waivers and the release of all our frozen funds, including those held in Qatar.”
Iran is also demanding recognition of shipping routes through the strait that it had discussed with Oman, and the closure of other routes, he said.
Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar Atas, reporting from Tehran, said there was “no remarkable flexibility in Iran’s position”, with Tehran insisting on the same demands while negotiations continue.
Under a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed between the US and Iran in June, Washington guaranteed the oil waivers and said there would be no further restrictions on Iranian oil exports, Atas said. But when the MoU collapsed months later, the US cancelled all the waivers.
Tehran is also still insisting on the release of its frozen assets, including $6bn held in Qatar, and on the lifting of sanctions, not only those on its energy and nuclear file, but also those imposed since the MoU collapsed, which are putting huge pressure on Iran’s economy, he said.
The US, for its part, wants Iran to reopen the strait, and both sides want their demands met on the ground, not only on paper, Atas added.
‘Prepared for all scenarios’
In his remarks to Al Jazeera, Araghchi said his country does not rule out the possibility of an attack against Iran.
“We are prepared for all scenarios,” he said. “We have upgraded our weaponry, addressed our vulnerabilities, and tested new arms. Our forces are at the highest level of readiness.”
Advertisement
This comes as Iran’s armed forces chief of staff, Major-General Ali Abdollahi, said in a statement on Saturday that Iran would respond to any attack with “immense force”, with no geographical limits, and that it would decide when any new war ends.
Abdollahi said Iran was acting on Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei’s orders.
“We have a new stockpile of enemy targets and assets, and they are on our agenda,” he said. “America and Israel will face an unimaginable response, and we are the ones who will determine the end of any new war.”
⁠US ⁠Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a press conference on Saturday that President Donald Trump has not yet made ⁠a decision on whether to ⁠resume military action against Iran. He added that he did not know whether there was a specific timeframe ⁠for Qatar-led talks ⁠aimed at resolving hostilities.
Abbas Khamayar, a former Iranian diplomat, told Al Jazeera he expects the current situation to hold until next week’s US midterm elections.
Advertisement

articles.title: Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky arrive in Ukraine via Belarus
articles.text:
Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky arrive in Ukraine via Belarus | Russia-Ukraine war News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Ukraine's Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets, centre, with residents evacuated from Oleshky after their arrival in Ukraine [AFP]
By Al Jazeera Staff and The Associated Press
Published On 31 Oct 202631 Oct 2026
Residents from the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, ravaged by years of war, have crossed into Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, after being evacuated via Belarus.
The evacuation is part of a major mission under a truce that the White House said United States First Lady Melania Trump helped broker last week.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 Melania or the pope: Who brokered Russia-Ukraine ceasefire in Oleshky?
list 2 of 3 Russia’s alleged sabotage campaign in Europe raises fears of escalation
list 3 of 3 At least 14 people killed in attack on Ukraine train stationend of list
The residents arrived in Ukraine on Saturday after leaving Oleshky a day earlier and travelling to Belarus. Neither Kyiv nor Moscow have confirmed the exact number of people evacuated.
Ukrainian and Russian officials visited Oleshky together on Friday, delivering aid and marshalling those who wanted to leave in a rare show of cooperation between the warring sides.
“As of now, Ukrainian citizens from Oleshky have crossed the Ukrainian border in the Chernihiv region. All of them will receive the assistance they need,” Zelenskyy said in a post on X on Saturday. “I thank the American side and US First Lady Melania Trump for their mediation.”
Four planes carrying the Oleshky evacuees arrived in the southeastern Belarusian town of Gomel on Saturday, said Ukrainian parliament member David Arakhamia.
The group was met in Gomel by rescue workers, medical teams and Red Cross volunteers, Belarusian state media reported.
From there, they were transported to Ukrainian territory.
The civilians from Oleshky, which has suffered from major food and medicine shortages after years of fighting, began the journey out of their region in bus convoys on Friday, under a rare regional truce that is expected to continue through Sunday.
People walk after disembarking a plane carrying residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky, in Gomel, Belarus [The Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Office/Reuters]
Russia and Ukraine have not specified how many people chose to leave the city, but Melania Trump posted on Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.

Those travelling to Ukraine were first bused to the Russian city of Anapa, before being flown to Belarus.
“It was a very long journey for them,” Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova said, reporting from Moscow.
“First, buses took them to Anapa on the Black Sea … And then they spent several hours getting to Gomel by plane”.
Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from the Ukrainian side of the border where evacuees crossed, said “a lot of preparation” was under way before their arrival, with a large media presence and humanitarian aid workers on site.
“Just a few moments ago, they arrived on about half a dozen buses,” said MacAlpine.
“As they arrived, they were given Ukrainain flags and Ukrainian bracelets. We saw some very emotional scenes. We spoke to one family, two daughters and their mother. They said their father was returning and that they hadn’t seen him for three years. We were with them in that moment when they saw him. There were a lot of emotions.”
Leonid Melnikov, a member of the Ukrainian Red Cross at the border site, told Al Jazeera that aid workers were expecting about 500 arrivals.
Evacuees bound for Russia
Russia’s ombudswoman and lead representative on the evacuation mission, Yana Lantratova, said buses also transported Oleshky residents who wanted to live in Russia.
Those residents were first taken to a temporary accommodation centre in Simferopol in the Crimea region, said Shapovalova.
Aside from the first lady’s apparent role in the truce and evacuation mission, Pope Leo XIV – the first American pontiff – also pressed Russian and Ukrainian leaders to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
“The Russian military provided safe passage and safe corridors for the evacuees and were de-mining the roads near Oleshky,” said Shapovalova.
Attacks continue elsewhere
Moscow and Kyiv continued to trade attacks elsewhere even as the Oleshky truce continued.
The governor of Russia’s Bryansk region said a Ukrainian drone killed two people and injured five in the settlement of Klimovo on Saturday.
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy said overnight Russian attacks hit Ukrainian power plants, railway infrastructure and a gas distribution facility.
The strikes left more than 200,000 households without power in the Dnipro region, and 80,000 more without power in the Kyiv region, he said.
Zelenskyy, who has long pressed partners to supply Ukraine with more interceptors, renewed that call earlier on Saturday, saying: “Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day.”

While Zelenskyy welcomed the US approval of Kyiv’s purchase of 500 PAC-3 Patriot interceptors, he warned that equipment could take years to deliver and that Ukraine’s military needs the supplies more urgently.
“The United States, our European partners, and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses,” Zelenskyy said in a post on X.
He urged allies to supply those existing interceptors immediately to cover Ukraine during the winter of 2026-2027, adding that partners could replenish their own stockpiles in subsequent years through the production already contracted and paid for.
